title: Where? — the place form
goal: Say where things are with *w* and *na*, recognize the *miejscownik* endings, and understand why some places take *w* and others *na*.
bekal: forming the *miejscownik* of the most common nouns
giving your address and where you work

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gdzie mieszkasz?
dialogs.intro: A bench on campus during the break. Ania and Budi swap stories about where they live.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: Where do you live in Kraków?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: W akademiku, na kampusie. A ty?
lines.id: In the dorm, on campus. And you?
lines.literal: in dorm, on campus. and you?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: In the center, on Długa Street.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Nie, dwadzieścia minut na piechotę. Pracuję też w kawiarni na rynku.
lines.id: No, twenty minutes on foot. I also work in a café on the main square.
lines.literal: no, twenty minutes on foot. I-work also in café on square.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: W Kolorowej. Jest w starym budynku przy kościele.
lines.id: Kolorowa. It's in an old building by the church.
lines.literal: in Kolorowa. is in old building by church.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Byłem tam raz. Siedzieliśmy na tarasie.
lines.id: I've been there once. We sat on the terrace.
lines.literal: I-was there once. we-sat on terrace.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Latem taras jest najlepszy. Zimą siedzimy w środku.
lines.id: In summer the terrace is the best. In winter we sit inside.
lines.literal: in-summer terrace is best. in-winter we-sit in inside.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A gdzie jest twoja siostra? W domu?
lines.id: And where's your sister? At home?
lines.literal: and where is your sister? in home?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Nie, jest na uczelni. Ma egzamin o dziesiątej.
lines.id: No, she's at the university. She has an exam at ten.
lines.literal: no, is at college. has exam at tenth.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Then I'll keep my fingers crossed.

notes: **Kraków becomes Krakowie, ulica becomes ulicy, kawiarnia becomes kawiarni.** Every noun after *w*, *na*, *przy* and *o* takes the form called *miejscownik* (the locative) — a form that never appears on its own without a preposition.

**This is the form that changes the most letters inside a word.** *Warszawa → w Warszawie*, *szkoła → w szkole*, *miasto → w mieście*. The reason is the same one you met with verbs: the *-e* sound softens the letter before it, and Polish spells that softening with a different letter.

**W akademiku, na kampusie.** Why one *w* and one *na*? Rough rule: *w* for things **inside** something, *na* for things **on top of** or on an **open surface**. In reality, some have simply become fixed habits — the list is in the extra section of this unit.
**Na ulicy Długiej** — addresses use *na*, and the street name changes its ending too, because it's an adjective (*Długa → Długiej*). With a house number: *na Długiej 15*.

**Byłem tam raz** — the past form of *być*, with the masculine ending *-em*. A woman says *byłam*. *Byłem w…* ("I've been to…") is so common that it's worth memorizing before the full past-tense rules in unit 17.

**Latem, zimą** — seasons used as time expressions take the *narzędnik* form you already know: *lato → latem*, *zima → zimą*, *wiosna → wiosną*, *jesień → jesienią*. One form, two jobs — more proof that Polish reuses its endings rather than piling on new ones.
**W której kawiarni** — the question word *która* (which) changes too, to *której*. Adjectives and question words always move in step with their noun.
**Trzymam kciuki** literally means "I'm holding thumbs" — the equivalent of "fingers crossed". Poles really do make a fist with the thumb tucked inside, instead of crossing their fingers.

grammars.title: Miejscownik — the form after w, na, przy, o
body: The form that answers *gdzie?* (where) and *o czym?* (about what). It only ever appears with a preposition — never alone.
after: There are only three endings: **-e / -ie**, **-u**, or **-y / -i**. What decides is the last letter of the stem, not the gender.

**The -u ending** goes on masculine and neuter words ending in *k*, *g*, *ch* and soft letters: *akademik → w akademiku*, *ratusz → w ratuszu*, *dom → w domu*. Words ending in other hard letters take *-e/-ie*.

⚠️ You don't need to learn the letter changes inside words (*miasto → mieście*, *szkoła → szkole*) as rules. Memorize the **finished forms** of the ten places you mention every day; the pattern will sink in through your ears.

grammars.title: W or na?
body: The main rule fits in one sentence, but there's a list of fixed habits to know — and the list is short.
after: The last row is the annoying one: *na poczcie* (at the post office) and *na uniwersytecie* (at the university) take *na* for no reason you can feel. Memorize the five most common and you're set for A1: *na poczcie*, *na dworcu*, *na lotnisku*, *na uniwersytecie*, *na rynku*.
If you pick the wrong one, you'll still be understood — it's not a mistake that changes the meaning. It just sounds like an accent.

blocks.title: Asking where things are
items: *Czy tu jest bankomat?* — Is there an ATM here?
*Jak daleko stąd?* — How far is it from here?
*Dwadzieścia minut na piechotę.* — Twenty minutes on foot.

blocks.text: These patterns answer almost every question you'll get in your first month. Swap in your own details, then read them aloud until they flow.

head: Polski
English
rows: I live in Kraków, in a dorm.
I live with a friend from Vietnam.
My room is small but comfortable.
*Uniwersytet jest niedaleko, dziesięć minut na piechotę.*
The university is close, ten minutes on foot.
There's a shop and a pharmacy nearby.
Before that I lived in Jakarta.

blocks.title: The Polish cities you'll hear most often
items: *Kraków → w Krakowie* (the old city in the south)
*Gdańsk → w Gdańsku* (the port city in the north)
*Poznań → w Poznaniu* · *Łódź → w Łodzi* — pronounced **wooj**, not "lodz"
